item.title: Nmap vs Masscan vs RustScan: Know Your Tools
item.content:encoded:
Three tools. Three different jobs. Most people are using the wrong one for the wrong task.

Series: Nmap — The Tool You Think You Know | Part 10 of 16

Nmap is not always the right tool. For raw port discovery across large IP ranges, it’s slower than Masscan by orders of magnitude. For initial CTF recon, RustScan quickly discovers open ports and can hand them to Nmap for deeper analysis. Knowing when to use which tool is what separates someone who runs nmap on everything from someone who runs engagements efficiently.

This article covers all three against a real target — Metasploitable2 at 10.38.1.119 — with actual timing numbers and real output. The table below uses actual timings from a lab target, not estimates.

The decision tree is simple:

  • Need raw discovery across many hosts? Use Masscan.
  • Need fast open-port discovery on one or a few hosts? Use RustScan.
  • Need versions, scripts, OS detection, or report-ready output? Use Nmap.

The Target

Before anything else, confirm the target is alive:

# ping -c 2 10.38.1.119
PING 10.38.1.119 (10.38.1.119) 56(84) bytes of data.
64 bytes from 10.38.1.119: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=22.8 ms
64 bytes from 10.38.1.119: icmp_seq=2 ttl=64 time=9.86 ms
--- 10.38.1.119 ping statistics ---
2 packets transmitted, 2 received, 0% packet loss, time 1000ms
rtt min/avg/max/mdev = 9.856/16.319/22.783/6.463 ms

Live. Now run all three tools against it and compare.

Tool 1 — Nmap

Nmap is the baseline. Full port scan with -p- and -T4:

Nmap’s strength is service and version detection, host hints, and deeper enumeration. No other tool in this article produces this level of detail automatically.

Tool 2 — Masscan

Masscan is a stateless high-speed TCP scanner. It sends SYN packets and listens for SYN-ACK responses — similar to Nmap’s SYN scan — but with no timing engine, no host tracking, and no service detection. It floods packets and records responses as fast as the network allows.

# Basic syntax
sudo masscan -p 1-65535 <target> --rate 1000 --wait 5
# Subnet sweep
sudo masscan -p 22,80,443,445,21,23,3306 10.10.0.0/24 --rate 3000
# Save output to file
sudo masscan -p 22,80,443,21,23,3306 10.10.0.0/24 --rate 3000 -oL masscan_results.txt

Masscan and virtual or VPN interfaces:

Masscan operates below the OS network stack, bypassing the normal TCP/IP implementation entirely. This makes it extremely fast on physical or bridged networks. However, it can have trouble with some VPN or virtual interfaces, such as tun0 or tap0 — unless you explicitly specify the correct interface and the environment supports raw packet injection. On setups like VirtualBox host-only adapters or OpenVPN tunnels, Masscan may appear to run successfully but return no results. If that happens, check which interface reaches your target with ip route get <target> and pass it explicitly with --interface. In some environments, you may also need --router-ip to point Masscan at the correct gateway.

On networks where it works correctly, a full 65,535-port scan against a single host completes in around 68 seconds at --rate 1000. A subnet sweep of 256 hosts across 7 ports takes roughly 25 seconds. The output below is representative of what Masscan returns on a routed network against a host with the same open ports our Nmap scan confirmed:

# sudo masscan -p 1-65535 10.38.1.119 --rate 1000 --wait 5
Starting masscan 1.3.2 (http://bit.ly/14GZzcT) at 2026-05-19 03:00:00 GMT

Notice what’s missing: no versions, no service names, no OS hints. Just IP, port, and state. That’s by design — Masscan is a discovery tool, not an analysis tool. You hand these results to Nmap.

The subnet sweep output saved to a file looks like this:

# cat masscan_results.txt
open tcp 22 10.38.1.119 1747619312
open tcp 80 10.38.1.119 1747619318
open tcp 21 10.38.1.119 1747619321
open tcp 445 10.38.1.119 1747619325

open tcp 3306 10.38.1.119 1747619342
#masscan
# grep "open" masscan_results.txt | awk '{print $4}' | sort -u
10.38.1.119

What Masscan cannot do:

  • Service version detection
  • OS detection
  • NSE scripting
  • Reliably handle rate-limited or slow-responding hosts at high rates

Tool 3 — RustScan

RustScan takes a different approach. Instead of replacing Nmap, it acts as a fast front-end for it. RustScan opens connections to all 65,535 ports simultaneously using async I/O, collects the ones that respond, then passes only those ports to Nmap. The result: Nmap never wastes time on closed ports.

Install — not available via apt on current Kali:

wget https://github.com/bee-san/RustScan/releases/download/2.4.1/rustscan_2.4.1_amd64.deb
sudo dpkg -i rustscan_2.4.1_amd64.deb
rustscan --version
rustscan 2.4.1

Full port discovery — timed:

The real 141.25s includes both the RustScan async discovery phase and the Nmap scan. The Nmap portion itself finished in 1.46 seconds because RustScan passed it only the 28 confirmed open ports — Nmap had no closed ports to test.

A note on --ulimit. On many systems, the default open file descriptor limit will throttle RustScan's async connections and slow it significantly. Passing --ulimit 5000 raises that limit for the session — RustScan applies it automatically when you include the flag, so no separate ulimit command is needed. It's a common tuning step rather than a strict requirement, but it's worth including on most scans.

Now pipe directly into Nmap with service detection:

rustscan -a 10.38.1.119 --ulimit 5000 -- -sV

RustScan discovers the ports, then Nmap runs -sV against only those ports:

Nmap portion: 14 seconds. Full-service detection on 26 ports.

You can pass targeted NSE scripts through RustScan the same way, without the noise -sC adds:

rustscan -a 10.38.1.119 --ulimit 5000 -- -sV \
  --script "banner,ftp-anon,ssh-hostkey,smtp-commands,http-title,smb-os-discovery,mysql-info,vnc-info,irc-info"

This gives you meaningful per-service enumeration — FTP anonymous login check, SSH host keys, SMTP commands, HTTP titles, SMB OS info, MySQL details, VNC version, IRC banners — targeted rather than broad.

What RustScan cannot do:

  • Standalone service detection without Nmap
  • Replace Nmap’s output formats
  • Work without Nmap installed
  • Consistently outperforms Nmap on single-port targeted scans

Speed Comparison — Real Numbers

All three tools against the same target, the full port range. Total workflow time is included where relevant:

Tool                             Discovery   Nmap portion   Service info
------------------------------------------------------------------------
nmap -p- -T4                     84s total   —              No
nmap -sV (targeted ports)        —           12.91s         Yes
rustscan --ulimit 5000           141s total  1.46s          No
rustscan --ulimit 5000 -- -sV    141s total  14.14s         Yes
masscan -p 1-65535 --rate 1000   ~68s total  —              No

A few honest observations from these numbers:

RustScan’s 141s total is the full wall-clock time from start to finish, including both the async discovery phase and the Nmap scan. The Nmap portion alone is 1.46 seconds for port-only output and 14 seconds for full service detection. If your goal is "time to get service info on all open ports," RustScan + -sV is the fastest complete workflow here.

In this lab, Masscan returned fewer ports than Nmap and RustScan. Stateless high-speed scanning can miss ports depending on rate, packet loss, and network conditions — this was observed on a local host-only network and may not reflect behaviour on other setups. The result is worth noting, but it is not a general rule. Masscan’s advantage is its scale: against a /16 With thousands of hosts, nothing else comes close.

Nmap’s 84 seconds is competitive on a local LAN. On a remote target over a real WAN, Nmap slows down noticeably while Masscan’s raw speed advantage becomes much more significant.

The Three-Tool Pipeline

The practical workflow for most engagements:

# Step 1 — Masscan for large network discovery
# Note: requires a routed network path — may not work reliably over VPN/TUN interfaces
sudo masscan -p 22,80,443,445,8080 10.10.0.0/24 --rate 3000 -oL masscan_results.txt
# Step 2 — Parse live hosts from Masscan output
grep "open" masscan_results.txt | awk '{print $4}' | sort -u > live_hosts.txt
cat live_hosts.txt
# Step 3 — RustScan for full port discovery on each live host
rustscan -a 10.10.0.5 --ulimit 5000 -- -sV
# Step 4 — Nmap deep scan on interesting targets
nmap -sS -sV -sC -O -p- -T4 10.10.0.5

Masscan finds what’s alive across the subnet. RustScan finds all open ports on specific targets and hands them to Nmap. Nmap does the analysis.

One practical note on passing multiple hosts to RustScan: the $(cat live_hosts.txt | tr '\n' ',') pattern works for small lists but can break with larger ones. For anything beyond a handful of targets, loop through the file or wrap it in a small script.

When to Use What

Scenario                                       Tool
---------------------------------------------------------------
CTF — single target, get started fast         RustScan → Nmap
Large subnet, find what's alive quickly       Masscan (needs routed network)
Authorized pentest, thorough recon            Nmap -p- then -sV -sC
Post-pivot internal scan                      Nmap only via proxychains -sT
  (Masscan and RustScan don't work
   through SOCKS proxies)
Need NSE scripts                              Nmap only
Need OS detection                             Nmap only
Need XML/grepable output for Metasploit       Nmap only
Running over VPN                              Nmap or RustScan
  (Masscan may not work reliably on
   VPN/TUN interfaces)

What’s Next

In Part 11, we flip the perspective completely. Instead of attacking, we look at what your Nmap scans look like to a defender — IDS signatures, log patterns, and how a blue team identifies scanning activity. Understanding this makes you a better attacker and a better defender.

Part 11← Link will be live once published

🔒 Legal reminder: All three tools covered here should only be used against systems you own or have explicit written permission to test.

Part of the series: Nmap — The Tool You Think You Know

Nmap vs Masscan vs RustScan: Know Your Tools was originally published in Level Up Coding on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: AI Benchmark Said It Was Better. Your Production Database Disagreed
item.content:encoded:
Generic LLM benchmarks measure language model capability. They don’t measure whether your AI SRE tool can still diagnose connection pool saturation after the upgrade. Those are different tests. And only one of them matters when your pager goes off at 2am in the morning

It started with a Slack message from the platform team.

“Hey, we’re standardizing on Gemini 3.5 Flash across all AI tooling in Q3. Cost optimization initiative. Vendor scored it highest on our internal benchmark suite. Rollout starts the 14th.”

Harris, senior SRE, read it twice. Eight months ago, Harris’s team had deployed an AI-assisted Ops agent for database incident response. It had been running quietly ever since — diagnosing connection pool saturation, catching autovacuum lag before it became a bloat emergency, flagging WAL slot accumulation early enough to avoid replication lag. Nothing dramatic. Just fewer 2am pages that lasted longer than they needed to.

Harris’s first question was not about cost.

It was: how do you know it’s as good at diagnosing our fault patterns?

The platform team’s answer was the benchmark score.

The Benchmark Problem

Here is what enterprise LLM benchmarks measure: reading comprehension, mathematical reasoning, code generation, instruction following, factual recall. Some measure multi-step reasoning. A few measure tool use in generic contexts.

Here is what they do not measure: whether a model correctly identifies connection pool saturation versus connection pool leak versus connection limit misconfiguration when looking at your specific pg_stat_activity output, your specific pool settings, your specific workload pattern.

Those are different tests.

An SRE choosing between models for an Ops agent based on a vendor benchmark is doing the equivalent of hiring a cardiologist based on their MCAT score. The MCAT is real. The score predicts something meaningful. It does not predict whether this specific cardiologist can read your specific echo.

The platform team’s benchmark said Gemini 3.5 Flash was better. Harris had no instrument to check whether it was better at the things Harris’s team actually needed it to be good at.

So Harris had little choice, but to approve the rollout.

The Quarterly Q3/Q4 Review

The rollout was clean. No incidents. The agent kept running. Pages kept getting resolved.

In the Q4 quarterly review, someone pulled the incident metrics. Mean time to diagnosis had drifted up. Not dramatically, not in a way that showed up in any alert. From 8.4 minutes to 11.2 minutes on connection-class incidents. Everything else was flat.

Nobody could explain the 2.8-minute drift. The model switch had happened in Q3. The hypothesis — connection pool saturation specifically was being misdiagnosed at higher rates with the new model, leading to longer investigation loops — couldn’t be confirmed because nobody had baseline cert data for the old model.

The benchmark hadn’t measured this. Nobody had.

Harris filed a task: “evaluate model performance on connection fault class.”

If you want to reproduce the findings presented in this blog post, please feel free to check out this doc page for details on the commands to run and their output, but the excerpts presented here should be sufficient to make our point.

What aiHelpDesk Would Have Shown

aiHelpDesk vault cert-compare reviews and compares triage diagnosis stability certs across two models. Side-by-side. A stability cert is not a benchmark score. It is the result of running the same fault injection N times under a specific model and measuring: did the agent correctly
identify the fault class of interest? Did it call the right tools? Did it produce a coherent diagnosis? STABLE means ≥ 80% pass rate with ≤ 30 percentage-point confidence range across repeat runs.

Every cert is scoped to a (fault_id, diagnosis_model) pair. This matters because it means cert-compare is not comparing models in the abstract. Instead, it’s comparing them on your specific fault catalog, using your playbooks, in your environment.

If Harris had run -repeat 5 on the connection fault class before the Q3 rollout…

faulttest vault cert-compare gemini-3.5-flash claude-sonnet-4-5 \
    --gateway $HELPDESK-GATEWAY-URL \
    --api-key $HELPDESK-API-KEY

…the output would have looked something like this:

  Stability comparison: gemini-3.5-flash  vs  claude-sonnet-4-5

  STABLE/UNSTABLE = triage diagnosis cert only 
  (keyword + tool + category scoring across --repeat runs; 
   remediation not included)

  FAULT                              OLD (gemini-3.5-flash)   NEW (claude-sonnet-4-5)   CHANGE
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  db-max-connections                 STABLE(5)  80%           STABLE(5)  88%            ✓ IMPROVEMENT
  db-vacuum-needed                   STABLE(5)  84%           STABLE(5)  82%            – EQUIVALENT
  db-lock-contention                 STABLE(5)  92%           STABLE(5)  94%            ✓ IMPROVEMENT
  db-tx-lock-chain-blocker           STABLE(5)  80%           STABLE(5)  80%            – EQUIVALENT
  db-connection-pool-saturation      STABLE(5)  88%           UNSTABLE(5) 61%           ⚠ REGRESSION
  db-wal-stale-slot                  STABLE(5)  80%           STABLE(5)  84%            ✓ IMPROVEMENT

  1 regression  ·  3 improvements  ·  2 equivalent  ·  0 not yet run

    db-connection-pool-saturation diag_rate: 88% → 61%  (Δ-27%)

One regression. One specific fault class. db-connection-pool-saturation. The precise fault type that drives connection-class incidents in Harris’s environment.

The benchmark said the new model was better. aiHelpDesk cert-compare said: yes, better at four things, equivalent at two and worse at the one that pages you at 2am.

Harris would have had a choice: roll out with a known regression and a mitigation plan, wait for a better cert on that class or keep the old model for connection incidents while using the new model elsewhere. Any of those is a defensible decision. What you cannot defend is not knowing.

The Model Name Is an Opaque String

One thing worth saying explicitly: aiHelpDesk cert-compare does not care who made the model.

The diagnosis_model (code link) field in the cert record is a string. It can be gemini-3.5-flash, claude-opus-4–5, gpt-4o or llama-3.1–70b-instruct. The comparison logic is identical. The STABLE/UNSTABLE threshold is identical. The output format is identical.

This matters because model selection in Ops is not a religious argument about vendors. At least it shouldn’t be. It’s supposed to be an empirical question about fault-specific diagnostic reliability. aiHelpDesk cert-compare is the instrument. The actual cert data that the cert-compare generates, answers this very question.

If your company signs an enterprise deal that mandates a model switch, from any vendor to any other vendor, aiHelpDesk cert-compare gives you the pre-promotion gate. You run it. The data tells you what changed. You promote with evidence or you push back with evidence. Either way you’re not guessing.

What Harris Does Now

Before any model upgrade or vendor switch, Harris runs a recertification pass (code link) on the fault catalog:

  # Certify the new model on all fault classes
  for fault in $(faulttest list --category db --ids-only); do
    faulttest run $fault --repeat 5 --agent-model gemini-3.5-flash
  done

  # Compare
  faulttest vault cert-compare claude-sonnet-4-5 gemini-3.5-flash \
    --gateway $HELPDESK-GATEWAY-URL \
    --api-key $HELPDESK-API-KEY

It takes about half an hour on a full DB fault catalog. It produces a table. Regressions sort first.

Harris presents the table in the migration review. The platform team sees it. If there are regressions, the conversation becomes specific and productive. It’s not abstract or guesswork anymore. It becomes about specific fault classes, specific pass rates and whether the business decision to switch models still makes sense given the tradeoffs. If there are no regressions, the switch gets approved faster because the evidence is there.

Nobody is flying blind. Nobody is defending “the benchmark said so” in a quarterly review. There’s evidence and confidence in making the right decision.

The Question to Ask Your AI SRE Vendor

Before your next model upgrade, planned or mandated, ask one question:

Can you show me whether the new AI model maintains diagnostic stability on my specific fault patterns or are you asking me to trust a benchmark that wasn’t designed for my use case?

If the answer is the benchmark, you are Harris in Q3.

The right answer is a stability cert table with your fault IDs, your environment, your pass rates and a column that says STABLE or UNSTABLE. As it applies to your company. Before you press deploy.

vault cert-compare is shipped with aiHelpDesk starting with version v0.20. The full workflow, from certifying a model, running a comparison and interpreting the output, is in the official aiHelpDesk documentation. The cert data lives in your auditd instance; no telemetry or any other information is sent to us.

aiHelpDesk is an open source AI-assisted incident diagnosis and remediation platform for SRE and DBA teams. aiHelpDesk invented and pioneered the concepts of Operational SRE/DBA Flywheel (blog post, doc), Triage Consistency Certification, Informed Consent, Second Opinion and Bill of Rights.

The vault commands, the Judge, the playbook diff, the full audit trail, the calibration data quality banner, the model-scoped stability certs and vault cert-compare… are not add-ons. They are the product. Trust is the product. The Judgment Layer covers what to do when the AI’s own improvement proposals fail. And why that case is where the most durable operational knowledge gets encoded.

Why aiHelpDesk Playbooks are trustworthy?

Because we give you, the customer, an ability to vet, verify and improve them through the methodology that we refer to as Operational SRE/DBA Flywheel, see here and here for details.

And yes, as a customer, you can not only confirm that the playbooks that you get with aiHelpDesk out of the box work for your environment, but you can easily bring your own. Both: BYO playbooks (by either importing your existing runbooks or cloning and customizing one of our’s or by creating one from scratch) + BYO faults as well.

Because nobody knows your specific databases, your environment and your workload with your upstream/downstream apps better than you do. You know how your database fails. Vendors don’t. At aiHelpDesk, we give you an option to create your own faults and add your own playbooks to triage and rectify them (in addition to the system playbooks we ship, of course).

And yes, we don’t depend on a particular model or a model provider. aiHelpDesk is model-neutral. From our standpoint, the LLMs are a disposable commodity. Flip from Gemini to Anthropic and aiHelpDesk should continue to give you exactly the same diagnosis and remediation. Anything shorter than that is a P0 bug.

item.title: Auto-Color Your Power BI Matrix: How to Generate Dynamic RGB Palettes using DAX
item.content:encoded:
A step-by-step guide to converting text strings into consistent, corporate-friendly pastel RGB values using a DAX hashing algorithm.

Every Power BI developer eventually runs into this formatting wall. You are building a beautiful project schedule, a release calendar, or a custom Matrix visual. You want every text category (like a product collection or status) to have its own unique background color.

The standard approach? You open the Conditional Formatting pane and manually create a list of Rules. If value is “Basic Line”, make background yellow. If “Spring Vibes”, make it pink. This works fine when you have 5 categories. But what if you have 50? Or worse — what if your dataset refreshes daily and a brand new category appears? Your carefully designed dashboard breaks, and the new category gets no color (or a random, jarring one).

It’s time to stop formatting reports manually. Here is how to force DAX to automatically generate beautiful, corporate-friendly pastel colors based entirely on the text string itself.

The DAX Magic: From Text to RGB Color

Instead of creating rigid formatting rules, we are going to write a single DAX measure that will:

  1. Read the text inside the Matrix cell.
  2. Convert the characters into a unique, mathematical identifier (a Hash).
  3. Use that identifier to determine the proportions of Red, Green, and Blue (RGB).
  4. Force those RGB values into high ranges (above 220) so the resulting color is always a clean pastel, never a dark or neon mess.

Here is the exact code. Just replace 'YourTable'[CategoryName] with your actual column.

Collection Color = 
VAR CategoryName = SELECTEDVALUE('YourTable'[CategoryName])

IF(ISBLANK(CategoryName), BLANK(),

    // 1. Create a unique hash from the text characters
    VAR Hash =
    SUMX(
        GENERATESERIES(1, LEN(CategoryName)),
        UNICODE(MID(CategoryName, [Value], 1)) * [Value]
    )

    // 2. Pick a color sector (0-Pink, 1-Yellow, 2-Green, 3-Cyan, 4-Blue, 5-Purple)
    VAR Sector = MOD(Hash, 6)
    
    // 3. Force high RGB ranges to ensure the color is always a clean pastel
    VAR High = 245 + MOD(Hash * 2, 11) 
    VAR Low  = 220 + MOD(Hash * 3, 11) 
    VAR Mid  = 220 + MOD(Hash * 7, 36) 

    // 4. Assign RGB based on the sector
    VAR R = SWITCH(Sector, 0, High, 1, Mid, 2, Low,  3, Low,  4, Mid,  5, High)
    VAR G = SWITCH(Sector, 0, Mid,  1, High, 2, High, 3, Mid,  4, Low,  5, Low)
    VAR B = SWITCH(Sector, 0, Low,  1, Low,  2, Mid,  3, High, 4, High, 5, Mid)

    RETURN
    "rgb(" & R & ", " & G & ", " & B & ")"
)

How to Implement This in Power BI

Once your measure is created, applying it to your Matrix is just a matter of a few clicks:

  1. Select your Matrix visual.
  2. Go to the Format pane and open the Cell elements section.
  3. Toggle on Background color and click the small fx button.
  4. In the dialog box, change the Format style from “Rules” to Field value.
  5. Search for your new DAX measure (e.g., Collection Color) and click OK.

The Result? Your black-and-white table instantly fills with consistent, beautiful pastel colors.

Why This Solution is a Game-Changer (Determinism)

The biggest advantage of this script isn’t just saving time during the initial setup. The real value shines when your data refreshes.

Because the RGB code is mathematically derived from the characters in the word, the text “Basic Line” will always generate the exact same color. Today, tomorrow, and next year. And when a brand new collection drops into your database, Power BI will automatically assign it a brand new pastel color without you lifting a finger. No more broken themes.

If you are a visual learner, check out my quick tutorial where I walk through exactly how to set this up on screen.

Found this trick helpful? Save this article for your next project and follow thebitoolbox for more advanced Power BI and Excel workflows!

item.title: How We Cut Infra Costs from $4,000 to $100 by Fixing Our Architecture?
item.content:encoded:
We cut infra costs from $4,000 to $100 by simplifying our over‑engineered AWS setup and moving to a leaner Railway‑based architecture.

Spoiler: We have decided to move our services to Railway but that was not the only reason we could save, by just moving the same services we could not reduce the costs 40x, main reason was many architecture changes!

Main Reasons We Have Achieved It

  • Simplifying the system, not designing for every possible scenario
  • Doing some trade offs, especially for consistency, some lags(minutes) in our Full-Text search is 100% tolerable.

Why Did We Go For Some Changes?

The Infrastructure costs were exceeding 4000$ and we got the request to review what is the cause, as first step I reduced the resources of Database and some other backend services deployed on AWS, but they did not have a large effect. it was obvious that we cannot change much with the existing architecture. another idea was to detach our services from AWS and make it deployable almost everywhere, including some bare metal servers and VPSs. we were using Railway for a few small services we have, and we were quite satisfied with what we have done there, also in terms of costs it was reasonable. so for doing the PoC I tried to extract pieces and deploy them on Railway.

The general main idea(also my intuition) was to go away from Serverless Database and Serverless Services in AWS to save some money. I tried to do a PoC on Railway to see the cost difference and the performance differences and if it makes sense to do some radical changes or not. during the process of detaching our setup from AWS I was trying out new ideas for each step that resulted in saving even more. In the article you are reading the big chunks that helped us save.

Why Moving to Railway?

  • Our services are now capable of being deployed anywhere, including VPS with solutions like Coolify.
  • Straightforward to use, in our opinion enough abstracted enough.
  • Better Project Level Separation of Costs for the many small Projects we have.

What Are We Doing? (Business)

This app is responsible for syncing an important entity to another software, then this data is going to be used for search and also making changes. let’s call it product. we have to keep an updated copy of these products in our system, we have to sync them to some other systems, the basic simplified functionality is this:

We have 12 Million of the same entity, on average we get maximum 1 Million updates per day that we need to handle, the amount of requests that we get from the clients, which are some mobile apps and web apps are not exceeding more than 100K per day.

We get into details of our setup on each one of the topics we discuss.

Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL(Serverless)

Approximate costs: 250–300$ per environment(3 environment: 750–1000$)

We were not doing massive operation, as I have said, max 1 Million records getting updated, also not boosts of thousands of requests per second, relatively smooth number of requests a couple times per day. the biggest mistake was that we were using the Serverless variations, and another mistake that we could have even fixed on previous setup was that our services were trying to keep a connection to the Database, as a result, our Serverless database could not shut down.

In the new setup, we have a normal PostgreSQL on Railway, we can tune the maximum amount of Memory and CPU, what we figured out is that we do not need more than 8GB of RAM or 2 vCPUs for primary.

Another good feature that helped us a lot in Dev environment is the Point in Time Recovery from Railway.

We still have normal backups everyday that we can deploy anytime(for now Cross Environment Backup Restore is not possible in Railway).

What I recommend for HA is this setup on Railway:

Deploy Postgres HA

How Could you Restore a Database on AWS?

When you try to restore a snapshot it creates a new cluster(new URL!) and the existing one remains as it is, it requires some extra steps until your services use the restored database, something that you do not want, we are doing some pilot migrations on a service last year and the most annoying thing that was happening to us was restoring the system state to a specific timeframe.

for more info check out this link(if you are a AWS expert and what I am saying is non-sense feel free to comment, I have the courage to admit and fix the article)

Recovery Point Objective(RPO)

On Railway our RPO is 60 seconds, with the PITR feature.(AWS Aurora offers even better than that it is couple of seconds)

Recovery Time Objective(RTO)

For Railway it is minutes to hours based on size of the Data, our Data is a couple of Gigabytes so probably it takes minutes. AWS Recovery time is also minutes.

Restoring a DB cluster to a specified time

AWS Database Migration Service

Almost 150$ per environment for DMS + Kinesis + Lambda functions (all together maybe around 500–600$)

We are using Elastic Search for searching our entities, so we had to

In the new structure, we are not reading the WAL stream, but whenever an incoming change is coming we write it first to our Postgres Database and if it succeeds then we write it to Elastic Search(the chances that writing to Elastic fails, does not differ much from the process we have in that Lambda function, in here at least we have a re-try process + we have a cron job to sync our Database to Elastic anyway). but anyway if we cannot write to Elastic successfully we log the specific event and the reason it failed.(we rely on our cron job to fix it)

Our cron job is doing an incremental sync, based on the field “updated_at” in the database, for the current load, it takes 15 minutes mainly because it is not finding a lot of mismatches between Postgres and Elastic.

If we change the Database directly, we have to execute our cron job to sync DB to elastic.

We are aware of the consistency issues, but we can tolerate the inconsistencies in the duration of each cron job(if there are any, so far we did not have the case) for making sure that DB is in Sync.

It’s okay if search results lag up to 5 minutes behind the source system and it is an intentional trade off we have made.

We could do the same thing on AWS as well and remove the DMS, Kinesis.

AWS ECS Fargate

~300$ per environment for this, around 1000$ just for ECS + Load Balancer + NAT costs.

Why ECS Fargate is expensive?

because it is serverless and usually 50–60% more expensive if we have the same resource on EC2.

Did it make sense for our traffic to use Fargate?

No, since we do not have a huge difference in load, it did not save us money, if we would have designed for the max number of requests we would have still save money.

We did not use saving plans; if we had, our AWS costs would have been lower, but still significantly above our new setup

Did we need 4 active instances at the same time?

Definitely not, we are not consuming more than 2GB of memory on the application, and we have never exceeded the 0.4 vCPU, this could have been improved on our AWS Setup as well.

Async Pattern in our Apps

This one was not that expensive, but still waste of resources. Lambda functions, specially our Lambda functions which were Javscript were just doing some network calls, or a Database call. we could do that in our main app as well.

In our new Setup we use Redis(But Persistent to not lose any job) and BullMQ to execute these jobs, no back pressure at all, we handle everything much quicker than the Lambda functions and we can handle our current load without back pressure or Event Loop Delay. For handling the jobs we did not see any abnormal spikes in our CPU and Memory of the main app, but the workers are decoupled and they can be deployed separately as another Nodejs app or a serverless deployment if we need to scale them separately.

Costs at the moment

We still have to shut down some services and remove the NAT and VPC on AWS, once we are done with moving everything over, but most expensive services are now running on Railway with the new architecture and the new setup is just 100$ a month, something that we could not believe at the beginning.

Was it all AWS’s Fault?

No in my opinion, we could have saved a ton by just doing these simplifications on AWS, but for sure we could not reach to such a number(100$). just having a VPC on AWS costs 50$ per environment.

Are We Satisfied with Railway?

It is super easy to deploy and use Railway, our whole team was able to adopt very fast to deploy everything on Railway, we have everything in just one place(logs, metrics, admin operations).

We can now distinguish different projects costs and charge business more accurately.

Railway experienced a few Incidents that mainly made the dashboard unavailable, or in another case the logs were loading slow but we were fortunately not affected by the recent ones, but something is clear, they are growing fast and I hope that reliability becomes their number 1 priority.

One major recent event:

https://www.reddit.com/r/webdev/comments/1ti37ys/railway_is_down/

Railway Status

Conclusion

For our steady traffic, designing for peak load was cheaper and simpler than building fully elastic, auto‑scaling infrastructure. If we can make some trade‑offs, we can go for a simpler design. Everyone should be explicit about the inconsistencies they can tolerate

How LLMs Were Used to Write this Article?

No part of the text is AI Generated, I have used AI to find typos and some mistakes, I used Google AI Mode Search to gather some information and do some double checks.
